text: Kristóf Szabó aka KristofLab presents his most critical project yet, Artificial Paradise. His practice explores the relationship between nature and civilisation, wilderness and urbanisation, and man's artificially created habitat: the city and its symbol, the tower block.

Artificial Paradise takes this further: artificially created natural spaces, domesticated and industrialised nature. Visions of the future that seemed utopian a few decades ago (a new relationship between nature and man, the possibility of total control) have become everyday practice.

Controlled, industrialised nature calls into question the very definition of nature. Can we still speak of nature when vegetation is artificially created and sustained, and functions as a visual element? How does this affect ecology and our image of nature?

KristofLab uses his usual multimedia tools (installations, videos, paintings and collages) to explore the bizarre, alienating nature of the phenomenon, and to envision the possibilities encoded in its present.
textCredit: Text by Luca Cserhalmi, aesthete. The exhibition was opened by Barabás Zemlényi-Kovács, theorist and independent curator.
behindTheScenes: This digital exhibition is a hand-built WebGL piece, written in vanilla JavaScript on Three.js and bundled with Vite. It has no game engine and no backend. The basement is generated procedurally from a small floor plan: walls, doorways, reveals and a stairwell are extruded from room rectangles, and brick, tile and concrete textures are painted into canvases at load time, so the 3D world itself downloads almost nothing. The artworks were extracted from on-site photographs with a perspective-correcting crop pipeline (sharp → WebP) and hung where they hung at MAMŰ. In Room 3, the projection is replaced by a live GLSL piece: a raymarch-free 2D shader that glitches between fbm foliage and a quantised grid of leaves and tower blocks. The ambient sound is synthesised with the Web Audio API (detuned drones, filtered room tone, a bar murmur near Room 2), and an AnalyserNode feeds its spectrum into the shader, the projector light and the post-processing (bloom, grain, chromatic aberration and a glitch pulse at every threshold). Everything runs at a capped pixel ratio with adaptive resolution, so it stays smooth on laptops and phones.

r2.blurb: The narrow warm-brick room with the bar, where the screens loop footage of glasshouses, geodesic domes and managed foliage.

r3.blurb: A long, narrow space. A white gallery of smaller prints opens through a curtain into a dark room: projected trees, a river of plastic, and the generative piece.
